newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Queensland's Surat Basin emerges as new coal giant.
newsitem.headline: Queensland's Surat Basin emerges as new coal giant.

text.p: The state government of Queensland has been inundated with expressions of interest from some of the world's biggest energy companies, eager to mine giant coal reserves lying under the Surat Basin in the central west.

The Surat, a long-time oil and gas producer, is now the key to one of Australia's biggest commercial ventures with nearly five billion tonnes of environmentally-friendly thermal coal waiting for energy-hungry Asian customers.
"We're looking at developments, not in the millions but in the billions of dollars," Queensland economic and development minister Doug Slack told Reuters in an interview.
That vision also includes the development of up to 50,000 hectares of agricultural land, mainly for cotton, Slack said.

Slack sees the undeveloped Surat Basin as the base for up to four new coal mines built and operating simultaneously, each producing three to five million tonnes annually and fed from one or two new power stations.

At the same time, in readiness for six to eight international consortiums, will be a new water supply dam project, rail links to the east coast and a new giant coal port development, possibly at the sugar producing centre of Bundaberg.

Already, up to 20 international groups have answered the state government's invitation for expressions of interest with a decision on the final numbers on both coal and agriculture to be made in September this year, Slack said.
The government is tight-lipped about who it had been talking to.

Analysts suggest the Japanese giants including Mitsui & Co, Mitsubishi Corp, Idemitsu and Sumitomo Corp along with Royal Dutch Shell, British Petroleum Plc and Peabody of the United States had all been in town.
"It certainly has attracted the big players but rail links and the port are the key to any firm commitments," Phil Hutchings of Brisbane-based broker Wilson HTM said.
"If those projects can be completed, then the Surat is a goer," he said.
Slack said his advisers have been told world demand for coal, especially for energy, was set to increase beyond the year 2000.
"Twenty groups or individuals or consortiums, conglomerates which include the major players have put in expressions of interest to develop the area," Slack said.
"Some are project specific," he said.
"Not only coal, there's a big area of land that has got agricultural potential, particularly for cotton," Slack said.
"There are some big players in the cotton industry," he said.
But irrespective of what emerges in the Surat Basin, Queensland's vast central land area will be developed, he said.
"Irrespective of what comes out, we will get water facilities, we certainly will get a rail link.
"And it's more than likely there will be a power station," Slack said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
